findings.explanation:
lightning-layout is a mobile-first 12-column grid. size sets the width at the smallest breakpoint and applies upward until a device-specific attribute overrides it, and the device attributes are additive: small-device-size means a phone, medium-device-size a tablet, large-device-size a desktop, and each applies to the size named and everything larger.
Three items at size='12' each take the full width, so on a phone they stack into three rows — the first requirement. To place all three on a single row from tablet upward, each has to occupy a third of the grid at the medium breakpoint, which is medium-device-size='4'.
The distractors each break one half of the requirement. medium-device-size='6' gives half width, so a tablet shows two items on the first row and the third below it — two rows, not one — and that stays true on desktop because the medium setting carries upward. Adding large-device-size='4' on top of medium-device-size='6' repairs the desktop but leaves the tablet at two per row, and the requirement names tablets explicitly. large-device-size='4' on its own leaves tablets inheriting size='12', so they keep the three-row phone layout.
One thing worth fixing in your mental model: size='12' never produces a single row on any device. Full width means one item per row everywhere, including desktop.

findings.explanation:
A queueable job is asynchronous, so nothing it does is visible to the test until the platform is told to drain the queue. Enclosing System.enqueueJob() in Test.startTest() and Test.stopTest() is what forces that: every asynchronous process started inside the block runs synchronously when Test.stopTest() is reached, so an assertion placed after it sees the job's results.
Each of the other three fails for its own reason. Enqueuing with no start/stop block at all leaves the job sitting in the queue when the query runs, so the assertion tests the state of the org before the job ever executed. Putting the assertion inside the block, before Test.stopTest(), has exactly the same effect — it is the stopTest() call that drains the queue, not startTest(), so an assertion above it is still running too early. And Database.executeBatch() is the entry point for a class implementing Database.Batchable; handing it a Queueable does not compile, because the two interfaces are unrelated.
findings.note: Item repaired; key unchanged at B. Treat the distractors as authored, not original.

findings.explanation:
Both A and B write the correct Status values, so the field values are not what separates them — read the placement of accountUpdates.add(a) instead.
In B the query itself is scoped: WHERE Type IN :statusMap.keySet() retrieves only Customers and Prospects, every record retrieved is one the rules apply to, and the new value comes straight out of the map with statusMap.get(a.Type), so the mapping is stated once.
In A the add() sits outside the containsKey guard, so every Account in the org lands in accountUpdates and the DML writes to all of them. The guard protects the field values but not the update. That matters in three concrete ways. Every one of those unrelated Accounts runs its update triggers, flows, and validation rules, so a single validation rule failing on a record that has nothing to do with this change fails the entire DML and nothing is updated at all. Their audit fields move even though no business field did. And the code does not survive volume: the unfiltered query is capped at 50,000 rows and the update at 10,000 records per transaction, so in an org large enough to care about this task, A throws before it finishes while B stays bounded by the number of Customers and Prospects.
C has the same defect as A in a more verbose form. D is the one that is wrong on values as well: it sets every Account whose Type is not 'Customer' — including Accounts with no Type at all — to 'Pending'.
The habit being tested is to scope the query to the records the requirement names, rather than querying everything and sorting it out in Apex.
